problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$

feedback.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $2{e}^{-t}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,s$ and $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡4\,s.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 2{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =-2{e}^{-t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=-2{e}^{-0}+C\,⟹\,C=2.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2-2{e}^{-t}.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡4\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=2-2{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=1\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)=2-2{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡4}=\frac{3}{2}\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {(1)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}-1 \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$
